disease_info: Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features is characterized by a major depressive episode accompanied by delusions and/or hallucinations that are typically mood-congruent, such as themes of guilt, worthlessness, or impending catastrophe. Clinically, it often presents with pervasive low mood or loss of interest, marked functional decline, and psychotic experiences that emerge as the depression deepens, sometimes leading to high suicide risk or severe impairment in self-care and social/occupational functioning. The course may be episodic, but psychotic features usually appear only during the most severe phases of depression and resolve as mood improves, helping distinguish it from primary psychotic disorders like schizophrenia. Careful assessment is needed to differentiate it from bipolar depression, schizoaffective disorder, and non-psychotic major depression, as treatment commonly requires a combination of antidepressant and antipsychotic medication, and sometimes electroconvulsive therapy in severe or refractory cases.

narrative.stressor: About six months before presentation, Ruth was promoted to a lead role in casino surveillance after a longtime supervisor retired, which meant longer night shifts, more responsibility for incident review, and pressure from management to cut down on losses. Initially she treated it like another challenge, juggling the new hours with her softball league and salsa classes, but over time she began dropping out of social activities and spending most of her off-hours alone in her apartment reviewing footage on her laptop. Around four months before seeking care, after a high-profile cheating investigation in which she worried she had missed key cues, she became increasingly preoccupied with the idea that the cameras were somehow "watching her back" even when she was off duty and that mistakes she’d made in the past were being silently recorded and judged, which eroded her confidence and made it harder to function on the casino floor. Coworkers noticed she was no longer her outgoing self and that she seemed fearful in the control room; she finally agreed to see a psychiatrist after her manager sent her home mid-shift when she became visibly distressed and insisted that security footage was being used to prove she was a danger to other staff.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t shake this feeling that I’ve messed everything up at work and that everyone can see how worthless I am, like it’s all being recorded as proof.”

narrative.stressor: Javon had been gradually winding down physically demanding handyman work because of chronic knee pain, and about five months before presentation he was diagnosed with early-stage heart disease after an episode of chest discomfort during a hike. His cardiologist recommended significant lifestyle changes and advised him to scale back strenuous activity, which disrupted his routine of pickup basketball, choir rehearsals, and hands-on car restoration projects that anchored his sense of purpose. Over the next several months he became increasingly withdrawn from church and community events, spending more time at home worrying about his health and interpreting normal bodily sensations as signs that his heart was failing, and he began to talk about the idea that his condition was a punishment and that he could hear God telling him he had "sung his last real note." When he stopped going to medical follow-ups and told his wife he didn’t see the point because his heart was already "done" and he was just waiting for it to stop, she brought him to an urgent care visit that led to a psychiatric referral.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I keep hearing this voice telling me my heart is going to give out and that it’s already too late for me.”

narrative.stressor: For years Claudia’s life revolved around coordinating arts and wellness activities at the neighborhood center and being deeply involved with her children and grandchildren, often hosting Sunday dinners and leading craft circles. About six months before she sought care, her youngest daughter moved several hours away for a new job, and around the same time the community center cut back its senior arts programming due to budget issues, leaving Claudia with fewer structured roles and less daily contact with people she felt responsible for. Over the next four months she pulled back from folkloric dance and walking club outings, spent more time alone at home, and began telling her husband that the house felt "empty" and that she suspected her family was slowly distancing themselves because she was a burden, occasionally insisting that she could hear them in the next room saying they would be better off without her when no one was there. After she abruptly stopped attending church and a close friend from the walking group visited and found her sitting in front of an unfinished watercolor, tearful and convinced her family was planning to abandon her, the friend persuaded Claudia and her husband to see a mental health clinic.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just don’t feel like doing any of the things I used to love anymore, even painting or going to my dance class.”
